summary: Describes an experiment under RFC 3933 in how the IETF forms working groups, called the Exploratory Group. Such a group is an early step between a BOF session and a working group, focused on prerequisites. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the IETF starts a new team, it tries a small trial group first to work out what the team is for. This describes that trial.

questions: what is an ietf exploratory group
how are ietf working groups formed
what are the ietf working group formation criteria
how long does an exploratory group last
subtitle: Early-stage work groups to test prerequisites for formal IETF team formation.

tldr.problem: The IETF working group formation process requires meeting multiple criteria before approval, and uncertainty about whether criteria can be met may delay or prevent group creation.
tldr.mechanism: Exploratory Groups are short-lived (6-12 months) test groups that focus on completing prerequisites for working group formation, providing formal recognition and tracking of progress toward the criteria.
tldr.outcome: This experiment, lasting 18 months from approval, permits the IESG to form up to three exploratory groups to test whether this intermediate step accelerates working group creation.

today: This experiment is an Experimental document. Its purpose was to test the exploratory group concept as an intermediate step in IETF working group formation.

sections.title: About Exploratory Groups
sections.content:
The Exploratory Group is an intermediate step in the IETF working group formation process. Before the IESG approves a working group, they check several criteria: that the topic is clear and relevant, that goals are achievable, that enough expertise and interest exist, that overlaps with other groups are understood, and other issues outlined in RFC 2418.

Sometimes these criteria are not yet satisfied, but the topic is promising. In the past, this often meant waiting months or years for answers, with no formal status. Exploratory Groups solve this by providing a brief, formally recognized period to complete the prerequisites for working group formation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a trial shift at a job: you get a little time to show you can do the work before they hire you permanently.

sections.title: When Exploratory Groups Are Created
sections.content:
An Exploratory Group may be created as a first step toward working group formation, or as an intermediate step between a Birds of a Feather (BOF) session and a working group. The IESG proposes an Exploratory Group only when relevance and interest have been demonstrated, but one or more of the RFC 2418 formation criteria are not yet met.

The charter for an Exploratory Group has two basic milestones: development of a working group charter and development of a document showing how the group meets the formation criteria. The IESG may include additional milestones such as a problem statement or requirements document, but must not include milestones for standards-track documents or protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The group gets a short list of tasks to complete: write down what the team will do, and show why the team is ready.

sections.title: Duration and Scope
sections.content:
An Exploratory Group is chartered for six to twelve months, with six months as the default. The IESG may extend an Exploratory Group by one additional six-month period, but extensions beyond that are not recommended. Exploratory Groups are treated like working groups in all IETF processes and infrastructure, with the exception that their names include EG to distinguish them from working groups.

An Exploratory Group is not a substitute for the existing working group formation process. It should be formed only when the prerequisites for working group formation are likely to be met if the exploratory group succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: The trial lasts about six months, and the team can ask for three more months once, but not again.

sections.title: The 18-Month Experiment
sections.content:
This RFC describes an RFC 3933 experiment running for 18 months from IESG approval. During this period, the IESG may approve formation of up to three exploratory groups. The IESG must announce to the IETF community in a public statement any decisions to form exploratory groups, including a description of each group that is formed.

Exploratory Groups are handled identically to working groups in IETF process, tools, and infrastructure. They use the same tracking and shepherding tools as other IETF documents, providing feedback and clarity on progress. The formation process includes review by the IAB and IESG, announcement of the potential group, and a request for community review.
sections.plainLanguage: For 18 months, the IETF will try creating up to three trial groups and track how well they work, using the same rules as regular groups.

sections.title: Measuring Success
sections.content:
Success of an exploratory group and the experiment is measured by progress toward working group formation. The primary metric is progress on basic milestones: whether the charter, formation criteria document, and other deliverables are completed within the specified time frame and whether feedback from the IESG, IAB, and IETF community is positive enough to lead to a working group vote.

Mailing list activity is a secondary metric. Active discussion indicates sustained participant engagement. An exploratory group with minimal mailing list traffic would not be a good candidate for milestone extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Success means the group finishes its tasks on time and people stay interested, enough that they are ready to become a real team.
